cards.english: I am a student. (nominal sentence — no 'am')
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has **no present-tense 'to be'**. Just place two words side by side:
**أنا طالب** (I [am a] student), **هي طبيبة** (she [is a] doctor), **الكتاب جديد** (the book [is] new).

produce.gloss: Just noun + noun. أنا طالبة (f).

cards.grammarNote:
**الـ** (al-) = 'the', attached to the front of the noun:
**كتاب** (a book) → **الكتاب** (the book). Before 'sun letters' (ت، س، ش، ن …) the **l** assimilates in sound: **الشمس** is said 'ash-shams', still written الـ.

cards.english: he is tired / she is tired (gender: ة)
cards.grammarNote:
Every noun and adjective is **masculine or feminine**; the feminine usually adds **ة** (taa marbuuta):
**هو تعبان / هي تعبانة** (he/she is tired), **طالب / طالبة** (male/female student). Adjectives agree with their noun.
cards.englishPhrase: He is a teacher, she is a teacher.

cards.grammarNote:
Possession is shown by **suffixes** attached to the noun:
**ـي** (my) **اسمي** (my name), **ـك** (your) **اسمك**, **ـه** (his) **اسمه**, **ـها** (her) **اسمها**. There's no separate word for 'my'.

Turn a statement into a yes/no question by adding **هل** (or **أ**) at the front:
**أنت طالب** → **هل أنت طالب؟** (are you a student?). Answer with **نعم** (yes) or **لا** (no).

produce.concept: هل turns a statement into a yes/no question
produce.answer: هل أنت طالب؟ hal anta talib?
produce.gloss: Put هل at the start; nothing else changes.

cards.grammarNote:
**أريد** (urid) = I want — followed directly by the thing:
**أريد ماءً** (I want water), **أريد قهوة** (I want a coffee). For 'I want to (do)', add a verb: **أريد أن آكل** (I want to eat).

produce.gloss: Polite version: أريد أن + verb.

cards.english: please (to a man / to a woman)
cards.grammarNote:
Politeness endings change with the listener's gender:
**من فضلك** (min fadlik, to a man) / **من فضلكِ** (min fadliki, to a woman). The same **ـك** vs **ـكِ** split shows up across 'your', commands, and greetings.

**أحب** (uhibb) = I like / love; for liking something in general, use the **definite** noun:
**أحب القهوة** (I like coffee), **أحب الشاي** (I like tea). Add a verb for 'like to do': **أحب أن أقرأ** (I like to read).

cards.english: The food is delicious. (adjective follows noun)
cards.grammarNote:
The **adjective comes after the noun** and agrees with it:
**الطعام لذيذ** (the food [is] delicious), **قهوة ساخنة** (hot coffee — fem. adds **ة**). A definite noun + indefinite adjective reads as a full sentence: 'the food is delicious'.

produce.concept: The adjective comes AFTER the noun (and agrees)
produce.gloss: Adjective follows the noun; agrees in gender & definiteness.

cards.english: I am at home. (في = in / at)
cards.grammarNote:
**في** (fi) = in / at — for being somewhere:
**أنا في البيت** (I'm at home), **هو في المدرسة** (he's at school). It's a nominal sentence: no 'am/is', just **في** + place.

produce.answer: أنا في البيت ana fi al-bayt
produce.gloss: Nominal sentence + في + place.

cards.english: on / under / next to (على / تحت / بجانب)
cards.grammarNote:
Common place prepositions, each followed by the noun:
**على** (on) **على الطاولة**, **تحت** (under) **تحت الكرسي**, **بجانب** (next to) **بجانب البنك**, **أمام** (in front of), **خلف** (behind).
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is under the table.

table.title: Common place prepositions
table.note: The noun after them usually takes الـ.

cards.grammarNote:
**هناك** (hunaka) = there is / there are (literally 'there'):
**هناك بنك قريب** (there's a bank nearby), **هناك مطاعم كثيرة** (there are many restaurants). Same form for singular and plural.

produce.gloss: هناك also means 'there' (place).

cards.english: I go to the park. (أذهب إلى …)
cards.grammarNote:
**إلى** (ila) = to / toward, used with motion verbs like **أذهب** (I go):
**أذهب إلى الحديقة** (I go to the park), **أذهب إلى العمل** (I go to work). The verb often comes first in the sentence.

cards.english: I am a doctor. (أنا طبيب — no 'am')
cards.grammarNote:
State a job as a nominal sentence, with gender agreement:
**أنا طبيب** (male) / **أنا طبيبة** (female), **هو مهندس** (he's an engineer). The feminine adds **ة**: **مهندسة**.

produce.gloss: أنا طبيبة (f). No verb needed.

cards.grammarNote:
Present-tense verbs change with a **prefix**: **أ** (I), **ت** (you/she), **ي** (he), **ن** (we):
**أعمل** (I work), **تعمل** (you work), **يعمل** (he works), **نعمل** (we work). The stem **-عمل-** stays the same.

cards.english: I work in a hospital. (أعمل في / كـ)
cards.grammarNote:
**أعمل في** = I work in/at (a place); **أعمل كـ** = I work as (a role):
**أعمل في مستشفى** (I work in a hospital), **أعمل كطبيب** (I work as a doctor — **كـ** attaches to the word).

cloze.prompt: I work in a hospital. (in / at)

cards.grammarNote:
For hobbies, use **أحب** + the **verbal noun** (the 'act of…'), usually with **الـ**:
**أحب السباحة** (I like swimming), **أحب القراءة** (I like reading), **أحب الجري** (I like running).

produce.gloss: Use the noun form السباحة (swimming), with الـ.

cards.grammarNote:
Feelings are nominal sentences (no 'am'), and the adjective agrees in gender:
**أنا سعيد** (male) / **أنا سعيدة** (female) = I'm happy, **أنا حزين / حزينة** (I'm sad).

produce.gloss: أنا سعيدة (f). No 'am'.

cards.grammarNote:
**أشعر بـ** (ash'ur bi-) = I feel + (a noun); **بـ** attaches to the following word:
**أشعر بالتعب** (I feel tired[ness]), **أشعر بالسعادة** (I feel happy[ness]), **أشعر بالخوف** (I feel fear).

cards.english: he is nervous / she is nervous (متوتر / متوترة)
cards.grammarNote:
Mood adjectives agree with the person's gender — feminine adds **ة**:
**متوتر / متوترة** (nervous), **غاضب / غاضبة** (angry), **متعب / متعبة** (tired). Match the adjective to who you're describing.

**جداً** (jiddan) = very — and it comes **after** the adjective, not before:
**متعب جداً** (very tired), **سعيد جداً** (very happy), **جميل جداً** (very beautiful).

Body parts take the same **possessive suffixes** as other nouns:
**يدي** (my hand), **يدك** (your hand), **رأسه** (his head), **عينها** (her eye). The **ـي** ending = 'my'.

table.title: Possessive suffix ـي = my
table.note: Attach ـي to the noun — there's no separate word for 'my'.

cards.grammarNote:
A common way to say something hurts: the body part (+ 'my') as subject + **يؤلمني** ('it pains me'):
**رأسي يؤلمني** (my head hurts), **بطني يؤلمني** (my stomach hurts). The verb agrees in gender: **يدي تؤلمني** (fem.).

produce.concept: Say what hurts: body part + يؤلمني (hurts me)
produce.gloss: رأسي (my head) + يؤلمني (hurts me).

cards.grammarNote:
The adjective comes **after** the body part and agrees with it. Non-human plurals take a **feminine singular** adjective:
**عيون كبيرة** (big eyes), **يد قوية** (a strong hand), **شعر طويل** (long hair).

produce.concept: Adjective follows the noun and agrees
produce.gloss: Object plurals often take feminine-singular agreement.

cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has a special **dual** for exactly two — add **ـان** (or **ـين**): ideal for paired body parts:
**يد → يدان** (two hands), **عين → عينان** (two eyes), **رِجل → رِجلان** (two legs). No number word needed.

table.title: Singular · dual · plural
table.note: Arabic has a special dual form for exactly two.

cards.english: the book vs. a book (الـ makes it definite)
cards.grammarNote:
**الـ** (al-) = 'the', attached directly to the noun:
**كتاب** (a book) → **الكتاب** (the book). The article never changes form in writing, always **ال**.
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.

b.gloss: definite — the book; add الـ to front

cards.english: Sun letters — the ل of ال assimilates
cards.grammarNote:
**14 sun letters**: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن.
Before these, the **ل** of **ال** is silent and the letter doubles in pronunciation:
**الشمس** (the sun) = *ash-shams*, **الدرس** (the lesson) = *ad-dars*.
cards.englishPhrase: The sun rises in the east.

table.title: Sun-letter assimilation examples
table.note: The written form is always ال; the l-sound assimilates in speech.

cards.english: Moon letters — ال is pronounced fully al-
cards.grammarNote:
**14 moon letters**: ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي.
Before these, **ال** keeps its **l** sound: **القمر** = *al-qamar*, **المستشفى** = *al-mustashfa*.

table.title: Moon-letter examples (ل stays)
table.note: Moon-letter words: pronounce the full al- as written.

cards.grammarNote:
**ش** is a sun letter → the **ل** of **ال** assimilates: *al-shāri'* → **ash-shāri'**.
Always written **الشارع**; the assimilation is only in pronunciation.
cards.englishPhrase: The restaurant is on this street.

cards.grammarNote:
**م** is a moon letter → the **ل** stays: **المطعم** = *al-mat'am* (full al-).
Moon-letter nouns: pronounce the article exactly as written — **al-**.

**د** (dāl) is a sun letter → **الدجاج** = *ad-dajaj*.
**ك** (kāf) is a moon letter → **الكتاب** = *al-kitab*.
Tip: if the letter is in the sun-letter list, the l doubles.

a.gloss: د is a sun letter — l assimilates

b.gloss: ك is a moon letter — l stays

cards.english: the big house (definite noun + definite adjective)
cards.grammarNote:
When an adjective **modifies** a definite noun, the adjective also takes **ال**:
**بيت كبير** = a big house · **البيت الكبير** = the big house.
Without **ال** on the adjective, it reads as a sentence: **البيت كبير** = the house is big.

a.gloss: the big house — both words definite

b.gloss: the house is big — adjective indefinite = predicate

cards.english: I like coffee (generic reference — use ال)
cards.grammarNote:
For liking something **in general**, Arabic uses the **definite** article:
**أحب القهوة** (I like coffee), **أحب السمك** (I like fish). This is different from English, which uses bare nouns for generics.

produce.gloss: Use الـ for the general category, not bare noun.

cards.english: Idafa first noun never takes ال
cards.grammarNote:
In an **إضافة** (possessive chain), the **first** noun drops **ال** even if definite:
**كتاب الطالب** = the student's book (NOT الكتاب الطالب).
Definiteness comes from the second noun: if it has **ال**, the whole phrase is definite.

cloze.prompt: the student's book — first noun gets ___
cloze.text: ___ كتاب الطالب is the correct form

cards.grammarNote:
**ص** (morning), **د** (lesson), **ش** (tea) are all sun letters.
**الصباح** = *as-sabah*, **الشاي** = *ash-shay*.
Rule: double the initial letter of the word in pronunciation when reading **ال**.
cards.englishPhrase: Tea in the morning is good.

produce.concept: Sun-letter rule: double the letter, drop the l
produce.gloss: ص، ش، د are sun letters — the ل assimilates.

cards.grammarNote: **م** is a moon letter → **المستشفى** = *al-mustashfa* (full al-). The hospital grammar card taught this. When in doubt, if the letter is **م ب ج ح خ ف ق ك ع غ ه و ي ا**, it is a moon letter.

cloze.text: المستشفى is a ___ letter, so al- is fully pronounced

cards.english: Quick reference: sun vs. moon for common words
cards.grammarNote:
Memorise by the article sound you hear:
**ash/at/an/ad** = sun letter → **al/ab/am/ak** = moon letter.

table.title: Sun vs. Moon — common course words
table.note: Sun: l assimilates. Moon: al- stays as written.

cards.english: Make definite: بيت ← البيت; شارع ← الشارع
cards.grammarNote: Add **الـ** to the front. For **بيت** (moon letter ب): *al-bayt*. For **شارع** (sun letter ش): write **الشارع** but pronounce *ash-shari'*.
cards.englishPhrase: The house is on the street.

produce.concept: Add الـ; then apply sun/moon rule in pronunciation
produce.gloss: ب = moon (al-); ش = sun (ash-).

cards.grammarNote:
**الطعام لذيذ** = The food is delicious (predicate sentence — adjective indefinite).
**الطعام اللذيذ** = the delicious food (noun phrase — adjective also takes ال).
The presence or absence of **ال** on the adjective changes the meaning completely.

b.gloss: noun phrase: the delicious food (adjective also definite)

cards.grammarNote:
**ص** (sād) is a sun letter → **الصباح** = *as-sabah* (not *al-sabah*).
Many learners mispronounce this; listen for the doubled **ss** sound at the start.
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee in the morning.

cards.grammarNote:
Most feminine nouns end in **ة** (tā' marbūṭa):
**طالب** (m.) → **طالبة** (f.), **معلم** (m. teacher) → **معلمة** (f. teacher). Pronounced like a short **-a** at the end.

table.title: Masculine → feminine (add ة)
table.note: Add ة to the masculine base to get the feminine form.

cards.english: Adjective agrees in gender with its noun
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic adjectives **agree** with the noun in gender:
**بيت كبير** (big house, m.) · **طاولة كبيرة** (big table, f.).
Rule: if the noun is feminine (ends in ة), add ة to the adjective too.

cards.english: Predicate adjective also agrees in gender
cards.grammarNote:
Even when the adjective is the **predicate** (after the noun in a sentence), it agrees:
**البيت كبير** (the house is big, m.) · **الطاولة كبيرة** (the table is big, f.).
No verb needed — the sentence is complete.

cloze.prompt: the table is small (طاولة is feminine)

cards.english: Some feminine nouns have no ة
cards.grammarNote:
Not all feminine nouns end in **ة**. Some are feminine by convention:
**أم** (mother), **يد** (hand), **عين** (eye), **أرض** (earth/land), **شمس** (sun). These are feminine despite no ة — adjectives still agree with feminine form.

table.title: Feminine nouns without ة
table.note: Adjectives agree: الشمس كبيرة (the sun is big).

cards.english: he is tired / she is tired (متوتر / متوترة)
cards.grammarNote:
Feeling adjectives agree with the person's gender:
**هو متعب** (he is tired) · **هي متعبة** (she is tired).
Just add **ة** to the masculine adjective to make it feminine.

cards.english: the food is delicious (masculine noun → masculine adj)
cards.grammarNote:
**الطعام** (food) is masculine → predicate adjective is masculine: **لذيذ** (not لذيذة).
Feminine equivalent: **الوجبة لذيذة** (the meal is delicious — وجبة is feminine).

cloze.prompt: the food is delicious (الطعام is masculine)

cards.english: the meal is delicious (feminine noun → feminine adj)
cards.grammarNote:
**الوجبة** (meal) ends in **ة** → feminine. Adjective must agree: **لذيذة**.
Compare: **الطعام لذيذ** (m.) vs. **الوجبة لذيذة** (f.).

cloze.prompt: the meal is delicious (الوجبة is feminine)

cards.english: هذا (m.) / هذه (f.) — demonstrative agrees in gender
cards.grammarNote:
Demonstratives agree with the noun's gender:
**هذا الكتاب** (this book, m.) · **هذه الطاولة** (this table, f.).
**ذلك** (m.) / **تلك** (f.) = that (far).

cards.english: she works / he works — verb prefix changes for gender
cards.grammarNote:
Present-tense verbs mark gender with prefixes:
**ي** = he · **ت** = she (also 'you m.').
**يعمل** (he works) · **تعمل** (she works).

table.title: 3rd-person gender in present tense (عمل)
table.note: يـ = he/they(m); تـ = she/you

cards.grammarNote:
State your job with gender agreement:
**أنا طبيب** (I am a doctor, m.) · **أنا طبيبة** (I am a doctor, f.).
No verb needed — nominal sentence.

produce.concept: Profession agrees in gender: add ة for feminine
produce.gloss: Add ة to طبيب to make it feminine: طبيبة.

cards.english: he is a teacher / she is a teacher
cards.grammarNote:
**معلم** (teacher, m.) → **معلمة** (teacher, f.).
**هو معلم** · **هي معلمة** — no verb 'to be'.
cards.englishPhrase: He is a teacher, she is a teacher.

produce.concept: Profession noun adds ة for feminine
produce.gloss: معلم (m.) + ة = معلمة (f.).

cards.grammarNote:
Borrowed words that end in **ة** are grammatically feminine:
**طاولة** (table), **سيارة** (car), **سلطة** (salad). Their adjectives take feminine agreement.

produce.concept: Nouns ending in ة are feminine — adjectives agree
produce.task: say: the table is small (طاولة = feminine)
produce.gloss: صغير (m.) → صغيرة (f.) to agree with طاولة.

cards.english: Non-human plurals take feminine singular adjective
cards.grammarNote:
In Arabic, plurals of **non-human** nouns (things, animals) agree with a **feminine singular** adjective:
**كتب كثيرة** (many books — not كثيرون), **بيوت كبيرة** (big houses).
Human plurals: **طلاب كثيرون** (many [male] students).

cards.english: Idafa = possessive noun chain (X of Y)
cards.grammarNote:
**إضافة** (idafa) = two nouns in a possessive chain, meaning 'X of Y':
**كتاب الطالب** = the student's book (lit. 'book of the student').
No separate word for 'of' — just place the nouns in order.
cards.englishPhrase: The student's book is on the table.

produce.gloss: No 'of'; just place nouns in order: book + the-student.

cards.english: First noun in idafa NEVER takes ال
cards.grammarNote:
The **first** noun in an idafa never takes **ال**, even if the meaning is definite:
**بيت الطالب** (the student's house) — NOT **البيت الطالب**.
Definiteness comes from the second noun.

cloze.prompt: the student's house — first noun gets ___
cloze.text: ___ بيت الطالب is the correct idafa form

cards.english: Idafa is definite if the last noun is definite
cards.grammarNote:
An idafa is **definite** when the second noun has **ال**: **مكتب المدير** = the director's office (definite).
An idafa is **indefinite** when the second noun has no **ال**: **مكتب مدير** = a director's office (indefinite).

b.gloss: indefinite — second noun has no ال

cards.english: ة on first noun is pronounced -t in idafa
cards.grammarNote:
In idafa, the **ة** (tā' marbūṭa) on the first noun is **pronounced** as a full **-t** sound:
**طاولة** = *tawila* alone, but **طاولة المطعم** = *tawilat al-mat'am* (the restaurant's table).

produce.concept: ة → -t pronunciation when first noun of idafa
produce.gloss: وجبة alone = wajba; in idafa = wajbat.

cards.grammarNote:
Idafa works for any 'X of Y' — places, names, categories:
**مطعم المدينة** (the city's restaurant), **صباح الخير** (morning of goodness = good morning).

table.title: Idafa in common phrases
rows: book of the student = student's book
table.note: First noun = no ال; second noun = ال if definite.

cards.grammarNote:
**عصير برتقال** = orange juice — an idafa with an **indefinite** second noun (no ال on برتقال): 'juice of orange'.
The whole phrase is indefinite: *a* juice of orange.

cloze.text: عصير ___ (no ال on برتقال because the idafa is indefinite)

cards.grammarNote:
Chains of three nouns are possible — only the **last** can take **ال**:
**مطبخ بيت الطالب** = the kitchen of the student's house.
All intermediate nouns: no **ال**, no possessive suffix.
cards.englishPhrase: The kitchen of the student's house is clean.

produce.concept: In a chain, only the final noun takes ال
produce.task: say: the kitchen of the student's house
produce.answer: مطبخ بيت الطالب matbakh bayt at-talib
produce.gloss: مطبخ and بيت have no ال; only الطالب has ال.

cards.grammarNote:
Adjectives can't be inserted inside an idafa. They come **after** the whole chain:
**بيت الطالب الكبير** = the student's big house — adjective **الكبير** follows the complete idafa.
cards.englishPhrase: The student's big house is nearby.

a.gloss: WRONG — adjective cannot split the chain

b.gloss: CORRECT — adjective follows the complete idafa

cards.grammarNote:
For pronouns (my, your, his…), use a **suffix** instead of a second noun:
**كتابي** (my book) = **كتاب** + **ي**. NOT **كتاب أنا**.
**كتابه** (his book), **كتابها** (her book), **كتابنا** (our book).
cards.englishPhrase: My book is on the table.

contrast.prompt: the student's book vs. my book

a.gloss: idafa — second noun is a full noun

b.gloss: possessive suffix ي (my) — no separate noun

cards.english: Build: قائمة الطعام (menu = list of food)
cards.grammarNote: **قائمة الطعام** = menu. Idafa: 'list (of) the food'. Note: **قائمة** ends in **ة** → pronounced **qa'imat** before the second noun.

produce.gloss: ة → -t before الطعام; no ال on قائمة.

cards.english: I work at the hospital (in a hospital)
cards.grammarNote:
Working 'at' a place uses **في** (in/at) + the place noun — not an idafa:
**أعمل في مستشفى** (I work in a hospital). Compare idafa: **مستشفى المدينة** (the city's hospital).

contrast.prompt: working 'at' a place vs. possessive 'of' a place

cards.grammarNote:
**وسط المدينة** = middle of the city = downtown. Classic idafa.
**وسط** (middle) + **المدينة** (the city). No ال on first noun وسط.
**قهوة الصباح** = morning coffee — idafa: 'coffee of the morning'. Note **قهوة** → **قهوت** (ة pronounced as -t) before **الصباح**.

produce.gloss: ة → -t before الصباح; no ال on قهوة.

cards.english: Dual: exactly two — add ـان / ـين
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has a special **dual** for exactly two: add **ـان** (nominative) or **ـين** (genitive/accusative):
**يد** (hand) → **يدان** (two hands), **بيت** (house) → **بيتان** (two houses).
No number word needed.

table.title: Singular · Dual · Plural
table.note: Dual -ān (subject) / -ayn (object/after preposition).

cards.english: Feminine dual: ة → ت before ـان
cards.grammarNote:
When a feminine noun (ending in **ة**) is made dual, the **ة** becomes **ت** before **ـان/ـين**:
**طاولة** → **طاولتان** (two tables), **وجبة** → **وجبتان** (two meals), **بيضة** → **بيضتان** (two eggs).
cards.englishPhrase: I eat two eggs for breakfast.

produce.answer: طاولتان / وجبتان (nom.) or طاولتين / وجبتين (after preposition)
produce.gloss: ة → ت before the dual suffix.

cards.grammarNote:
**بيرة** (beer, f.) → **بيرتان** (two beers, nominative).
Use **بيرتين** (birratayn) when it is the object or follows a preposition:
**أريد بيرتين** (I want two beers).

cloze.prompt: two beers (بيرة is feminine) — nominative form

cards.english: Broken plurals change the internal vowel pattern
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic **broken plurals** (جمع التكسير) change the root's vowel pattern rather than adding a suffix:
**كتاب** (book) → **كتب** (kutub, books). Each pattern must be memorised with the noun.
cards.englishPhrase: The books are on the table.

table.title: Common broken plural patterns
table.note: Broken plurals must be memorised — there is no single rule.

cards.grammarNote:
Many feminine nouns (and some borrowed words) form plurals by adding **ـات** (-āt), dropping the **ة**:
**وجبة** → **وجبات** (meals), **مشكلة** → **مشكلات** (problems).

table.title: Sound feminine plural (-at)
table.note: Drop ة, add ـات. Adjective agrees with feminine singular.

cards.english: Sound masculine plural: add ـون / ـين
cards.grammarNote:
Human masculine nouns often take **ـون** (nominative) / **ـين** (genitive/accusative):
**معلم** → **معلمون / معلمين** (teachers, m.).
Non-human plurals take broken or ـات forms instead.

**بيت** (house) → broken plural **بيوت** (buyut).
The vowel pattern shifts: b-ay-t → b-u-y-ū-t. This must be memorised.
cards.englishPhrase: There are many houses on the street.

cards.grammarNote:
**مطعم** (restaurant) → broken plural **مطاعم** (mata'im).
Many **مَفعَل** pattern words use **مَفَاعِل** as their plural: **مكتب → مكاتب**, **مطعم → مطاعم**.

**Non-human** plurals (things, animals) always take a **feminine singular** adjective:
**مطاعم كثيرة** (many restaurants), **بيوت كبيرة** (big houses).
This is one of the most important rules of Arabic agreement.

produce.gloss: كثيرة (f.sg.) not كثيرون — non-human rule.

cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has **collective** nouns (the category) and **unit** nouns (one item, with **ة**):
**سمك** (fish in general) · **سمكة** (one fish). **خبز** (bread) · **خبزة** (a loaf).
Use the collective for 'fish as food'; the unit for one piece.

Broken plurals must be learnt word by word. Common patterns:
**فَعَل → أَفعَال**: شخص → أشخاص
**فَعِيل → فُعَلَاء**: طبيب → أطباء
**مَفعَل → مَفَاعِل**: مطعم → مطاعم
cards.englishPhrase: The doctors work in the hospital.

table.title: Broken plurals from known words
table.note: Each must be memorised — no single rule covers all.

cards.grammarNote:
**عين** (eye, f.) → **عينان** (two eyes, nominative) · **عينين** (genitive/accusative).
**عين** is irregular: it is feminine without **ة**, so no consonant change before the dual suffix.

produce.task: give dual and plural of عين (eye)
produce.gloss: Dual = exactly two; broken plural = three or more.

cards.grammarNote:
**بيضة** (egg, f.) → dual **بيضتان** (nominative) / **بيضتين** (after preposition/as object).
In **في الفطور** = at breakfast, the dual takes the **ـين** form.
cards.englishPhrase: I eat two eggs for breakfast.

cloze.prompt: two eggs (object/after prep) — which dual form?

cards.english: Past tense: add person suffixes to the root
cards.grammarNote:
The Arabic **past tense** (الماضي) is built by adding suffixes to the root form. The 3rd-person masculine singular (**هو**) is the base form used in dictionaries:
**عمل** ('amila) = he worked.

table.title: Past tense: عمل (to work) — full paradigm
table.note: Suffixes attach to the root: -tu (I), -ta (you m), -ti (you f), -na (we), -u (they m).

cards.grammarNote:
First-person singular past = root + **تُ** (-tu):
**عمل + تُ → عملتُ** (I worked), **ذهب + تُ → ذهبتُ** (I went), **أكل + تُ → أكلتُ** (I ate).
cards.englishPhrase: I worked in the office yesterday.

cards.grammarNote:
First-person plural past = root + **نا** (-na):
**أكل + نا → أكلنا** (we ate), **ذهب + نا → ذهبنا** (we went), **عمل + نا → عملنا** (we worked).

cards.english: she worked vs. he worked (past, gender)
cards.grammarNote:
3rd person singular past:
**هو عمل** (he worked) = bare root.
**هي عملت** (she worked) = root + **ـتْ** (-at).
The **ت** marks feminine in the past tense.

**ذهب** (to go) in the past:
**ذهبتُ** (I went), **ذهبتَ** (you went, m.), **ذهب** (he went), **ذهبت** (she went), **ذهبنا** (we went), **ذهبوا** (they went).

table.title: ذهب (to go) — past tense
table.note: Same suffix pattern as عمل.

cards.grammarNote:
**أكل** (to eat) → past:
**أكلتُ** (I ate), **أكلنا** (we ate), **أكلوا** (they ate).
The **أ** (hamza) at the start doesn't change in the past tense.

produce.task: give past 1sg of: أكل (eat) and ذهب (go)
produce.gloss: Add تُ to the root: أكل + تُ = أكلتُ.

cards.english: They went / they ate (3rd plural past)
cards.grammarNote:
3rd person masculine plural past = root + **وا** (-ū):
**ذهبوا** (they went), **أكلوا** (they ate), **عملوا** (they worked).
The **وا** is the standard masculine plural past suffix.

cloze.prompt: they went (3rd pl past) — root ذهب + ___

cards.grammarNote:
To negate a past action, Arabic does NOT use a past verb. Instead:
**لم** + present jussive (no prefix vowel on the verb):
**لم يذهب** (he did not go), **لم آكل** (I did not eat).
The verb after **لم** takes a shortened jussive form.
cards.englishPhrase: He did not go to the office.

b.gloss: he did not go — لم + jussive present

cards.grammarNote:
In a verbal sentence (جملة فعلية), the **verb comes first**, then subject, then object:
**أكل الطالب الطعام** (the student ate the food).
When the verb precedes a plural subject, it stays in the singular form.

produce.concept: Verbal sentence order: verb → subject → object
produce.task: say: the student ate the food (verb-first)
produce.gloss: Verb first; verb stays singular even if subject is plural.

cards.grammarNote:
**شرب** (to drink) → past 1sg: **شربتُ** (I drank).
Past 3rd m sg: **شرب** (he drank). Past 3rd f sg: **شربت** (she drank).

cards.english: Build: We went to the hospital
cards.grammarNote:
**ذهب + نا → ذهبنا** (we went) + **إلى المستشفى** (to the hospital).
Past 1pl suffix **نا** attached to root **ذهب**.

produce.task: say: we went to the hospital
produce.answer: ذهبنا إلى المستشفى dhahabna ila al-mustashfa
produce.gloss: ذهب + نا = ذهبنا (we went).

cards.grammarNote:
**هي** past = root + **تْ** (-at): **أكلت** (she ate).
Note: **أكلتُ** (I ate) looks similar but ends in a vowel (**تُ** = -tu) while **أكلتْ** (she ate) has a sukun on the **ت** (-t) — a subtle but important distinction in MSA.

cards.english: Time words with the past: أمس (yesterday)
cards.grammarNote:
Common time words used with the past tense:
**أمس** (ams) = yesterday · **هذا الصباح** (this morning) · **الأسبوع الماضي** (last week).
They typically come at the start or end of the sentence.

table.title: Time words for the past
table.note: Place at start or end of sentence.

cards.english: Present tense: prefixes mark person & gender
cards.grammarNote:
The Arabic **present tense** (المضارع) is formed by adding prefixes (and sometimes suffixes) to the root:
**أ** (I) · **ت** (you/she) · **ي** (he) · **ن** (we).
The stem stays constant: **-عمل-** (work).

table.title: Present tense: عمل (to work)
table.note: Prefix: أ-/ت-/ي-/ن-. Fem you adds -in suffix.

cards.english: I work vs. we work (prefix أ / ن)
cards.grammarNote:
**أ** prefix = I: **أعمل** (I work), **آكل** (I eat), **أذهب** (I go).
**ن** prefix = we: **نعمل** (we work), **نأكل** (we eat), **نذهب** (we go).
cards.englishPhrase: We go to the park every day.

cards.english: he works / she works (ي vs ت prefix)
cards.grammarNote:
**ي** prefix = he (3rd m sg): **يعمل** (he works).
**ت** prefix = she (3rd f sg) OR you (2nd m/f sg): **تعمل** (she works / you work).
Context resolves ambiguity.

The feminine 'you' (2nd f sg) adds **ـين** (-īn) to the stem:
**تعملين** (you work, f.), **تذهبين** (you go, f.), **تأكلين** (you eat, f.).
Masculine 'you': **تعمل** (no extra suffix).

a.gloss: you work — masculine, no extra suffix

cards.grammarNote:
3rd person masculine plural: prefix **ي** + stem + suffix **ون** (-ūn):
**يعملون** (they work), **يذهبون** (they go), **يأكلون** (they eat).

produce.task: give they-form for: عمل (work) and ذهب (go)
produce.gloss: ي + root + ون for 3rd m pl.

cards.english: Indicative mood: final ـُ on the verb
cards.grammarNote:
The **indicative** (المرفوع) is the default present mood, with a **ḍamma** (ـُ) ending on the verb:
**يعملُ** (he works — indicative). Other moods change this ending.

table.title: Three present moods (3sg m, root عمل)
table.note: In everyday speech, the mood endings are often dropped.

cards.english: أن + subjunctive: I want to eat
cards.grammarNote:
After **أن** (an, 'that/to'), the verb takes the **subjunctive** (منصوب), with a **fatḥa** (ـَ) ending:
**أريد أن آكلَ** (I want to eat), **أحب أن أذهبَ** (I like to go).
In practice, the vowel endings are often silent in speech.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to go to the restaurant.

produce.concept: أن + verb = to (do): أريد أن + verb
produce.answer: أريد أن آكل urid an akul
produce.gloss: أريد (I want) + أن (to) + آكل (eat, subjunctive).

cards.english: لم + jussive: he did not work
cards.grammarNote:
**لم** (lam) = did not (past negation) + **jussive** (مجزوم), with a **sukūn** (ـْ) ending:
**لم يعملْ** (he did not work), **لم أذهبْ** (I did not go).
The verb after **لم** is present-tense in form but past in meaning.
cards.englishPhrase: I did not go to the office.

a.gloss: he does not work — present negation

b.gloss: he did not work — لم + jussive

cards.grammarNote:
**لا** (lā) + indicative present = does not/don't:
**لا أعرف** (I don't know), **لا يأكل اللحم** (he doesn't eat meat), **لا أفهم** (I don't understand).

The prefix **سـ** (sa-) on a present verb marks the **near future**:
**سأذهب** (I will go), **سنأكل** (we will eat), **سيعمل** (he will work).
The longer form **سوف** (sawfa) is also used (slightly more formal).
cards.englishPhrase: I will go to the restaurant.

produce.task: say: I will eat at the restaurant
produce.answer: سآكل في المطعم sa-akul fi al-mat'am
produce.gloss: سـ + آكل (I eat) = سآكل (I will eat).

cards.english: he goes (يذهب) — present prefix for he
cards.grammarNote:
**يذهب** (yadhhab) = he goes. The **ي** prefix marks 3rd person masculine.
Remember: the same prefix **ي** is used for **he** in ALL present-tense verbs.

In Arabic, the verb already shows person/gender, so the pronoun is **optional**:
**أعمل هنا** (I work here) = **أنا أعمل هنا**.
Drop the pronoun when no emphasis is needed.

cards.english: Full present paradigm: three known verbs
cards.grammarNote:
The prefix pattern is the same across all sound verbs. Memorise the prefix, then plug in any root:
**أ/ت/ي/ن** + root + (suffix for f/pl).
cards.englishPhrase: We drink tea in the morning.

table.title: I/you(m)/he/we — three verbs
table.note: Prefix: أ- (I), تـ- (you/she), يـ- (he), نـ- (we). Stem stays same.

cards.english: Arabic verb forms: root + pattern = meaning
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic verbs are built from a **3-letter root** placed into one of **10 standard patterns** (أوزان).
The pattern adds a predictable layer of meaning. Root **ع-م-ل** (work) in different forms → different meanings.

table.title: Forms I–IV at a glance (root ع-م-ل)
table.note: Each pattern adds a layer of meaning to the same root.

cards.grammarNote:
**Form I** is the basic verb form — the root itself with simple vowels:
**ذهب** (he went), **شرب** (he drank), **أكل** (he ate), **عمل** (he worked), **فهم** (he understood).
Three vowel patterns: فَعَلَ / فَعِلَ / فَعُلَ — must be learnt per verb.

produce.task: give Form I past for: go, drink, eat, work
produce.gloss: Form I: root vowels only, no prefix/doubling.

cards.grammarNote:
**Form II** doubles the middle root letter (**تشديد**), giving an **intensive or causative** meaning:
**علّم** ('allama, he taught — from root ع-ل-م, to know → to cause to know),
**قدّم** (qaddama, he presented/served),
**طبّخ** (tabbakha, he cooked intensively).

contrast.prompt: Form I vs. Form II (root ع-ل-م)

b.gloss: Form II — he taught (causative: caused to know)

cards.grammarNote:
**Form III** lengthens the first vowel (فَاعَلَ), conveying action **directed toward** or **with** another person:
**سافر** (safara, he traveled — from س-ف-ر),
**غادر** (ghadara, he departed — from غ-د-ر),
**عامل** (amala, he dealt/treated someone).

table.title: Form III examples (from known roots)
table.note: Form III: long vowel after first root letter.

cards.english: Form IV (أَفعَلَ) — causative with prefix أ
cards.grammarNote:
**Form IV** adds **أَ** prefix with short first vowel, giving **causative** meaning:
**أقام** (aqama, he caused to stand/resided — from ق-و-م),
**أحضر** (ahdara, he brought — from ح-ض-ر, to be present → to cause to be present).

contrast.prompt: Form I vs. Form IV (root ح-ض-ر)

b.gloss: Form IV — he brought (caused to be present)

cards.english: Form V (تَفَعَّلَ) — reflexive of Form II
cards.grammarNote:
**Form V** adds **تَ** prefix to Form II, giving a **reflexive** meaning (the action happens to the subject):
**تكلّم** (takallama, he spoke — root ك-ل-م: word → he verbalized himself),
**توقّف** (tawaqqafa, he stopped — root و-ق-ف: cause to stop → stop oneself).

cloze.prompt: تكلّم (to speak) = Form ___ of root ك-ل-م

cards.grammarNote:
**Form VI** is the reflexive of Form III — two parties acting **on each other**:
**تعاون** (ta'awana, they cooperated — عون, help, mutual helping),
**تقابل** (taqabala, they met face to face — reciprocal facing).

contrast.prompt: Form III vs. Form VI (root ق-ب-ل)

a.gloss: Form III — he met (one person meets another)

b.gloss: Form VI — they met each other (mutual)

cards.grammarNote:
**Form VII** adds **ان** prefix, giving a **passive or involuntary** meaning:
**انكسر** (inkasara, it broke — root ك-س-ر: to break → to be broken),
**انفتح** (infataha, it opened up — root ف-ت-ح: to open → to open itself).

produce.gloss: ان + كسر = انكسر (passive: broke on its own).

cards.grammarNote:
**Form VIII** inserts **ت** after the first root letter (افتعل):
**اجتمع** (ijtama'a, he gathered — root ج-م-ع),
**التقى** (iltaqa, he met — root ل-ق-ي),
**انتظر** (intazara, he waited — root ن-ظ-ر).

table.title: Form VIII examples from the course
table.note: Form VIII: ا + root1 + ت + root2&3.

cards.grammarNote:
**Form X** adds **استـ** prefix — meaning 'to consider X to be, to request, or to be able':
**استطاع** (istata'a, he was able — root ط-و-ع: obedient → found it possible),
**استغرق** (istaghraqa, it took/lasted — root غ-ر-ق).

contrast.prompt: Form I vs. Form X (root ط-و-ع)

b.gloss: Form X — he was able (found himself capable)

cards.english: Masdar (verbal noun) derives from each form
cards.grammarNote:
Each verb form has a **masdar** (verbal noun, مصدر) that acts like an English infinitive:
**Form I ذهب → ذهاب** (going), **Form II علّم → تعليم** (teaching), **Form V تكلّم → تكلّم** (speaking), **Form X استطاع → استطاعة** (ability).

table.title: Masdars from known forms
table.note: Masdar = verbal noun; used like English infinitive.

cards.grammarNote:
Each form has an **active participle** (اسم الفاعل) — the noun 'one who does':
**Form I** pattern: **فاعل** → **طالب** (seeker = student), **نادل** (one who serves = waiter).
**Form II** pattern: **مُفَعِّل** → **معلّم** (one who teaches = teacher).
cards.englishPhrase: The student is in the library.

table.title: Active participles from course words
rows: Form I fa'il — student (one who seeks)
Form I fa'il — waiter (one who serves)
Form IV muf'il — manager (one who runs)
table.note: Active participle = the doer. Form determines the pattern.

cards.english: Passive participle (مفعول) = that which is done
cards.grammarNote:
**Form I passive participle** pattern: **مَفعول** — 'the thing acted upon':
**مطبوخ** (cooked — from طبخ), **مكتوب** (written — from كتب), **مشروب** (a drink — from شرب).
These also function as adjectives: **الدجاج مطبوخ** (the chicken is cooked).

produce.task: give passive participle for: شرب (drink) and طبخ (cook)
produce.gloss: Pattern: مـ + root1 + ـفـ + ـو + root3 → مفعول.

cards.english: Forms II vs. V: teaching vs. speaking
cards.grammarNote:
A famous trio from root ع-ل-م and ك-ل-م:
**علّم** (Form II: he taught), **تعلّم** (Form V: he learned — reflexive of teaching),
**تكلّم** (Form V of ك-ل-م: he spoke — reflexive of speaking).

contrast.prompt: Form II vs. Form V (root ع-ل-م)

b.gloss: Form V — he learned (reflexive: taught himself)

cards.english: Nominal sentence: no verb — noun/adj as predicate
cards.grammarNote:
A **جملة اسمية** (nominal sentence) starts with a noun or pronoun and has no present-tense 'to be':
**أنا طالب** (I am a student), **الطعام لذيذ** (the food is delicious), **البيت كبير** (the house is big).

produce.concept: Nominal sentence: subject + predicate, no verb
produce.task: say: the house is big (no verb)
produce.gloss: No 'is' — just subject + predicate adjective.

cards.grammarNote:
A **جملة فعلية** (verbal sentence) starts with a **conjugated verb**:
**يعمل الطالب** (the student works), **ذهب الطالب** (the student went), **أكل الطالب الطعام** (the student ate the food).
When the verb comes before the subject, it agrees in gender but stays singular even if the subject is plural.
cards.englishPhrase: The student works in the office.

cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has no present-tense equivalent of 'is/am/are'. Instead, noun + predicate directly:
**البيت كبير** (the house is big), **هو معلم** (he is a teacher), **القهوة ساخنة** (the coffee is hot).

produce.concept: No 'is' in Arabic — subject + predicate only
produce.gloss: Just noun + adjective — no verb.

cards.grammarNote:
The predicate in a nominal sentence can be a **prepositional phrase**:
**الكتاب على الطاولة** (the book is on the table), **القطة تحت الطاولة** (the cat is under the table).
No verb needed — the preposition phrase serves as the predicate.
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.

produce.concept: Prep phrase as predicate: subject + في/على/تحت + place
produce.task: say: the cat is under the table
produce.answer: القطة تحت الطاولة al-qitta taht at-tawila
produce.gloss: No verb — تحت الطاولة is the predicate.

cards.english: Verbal sentence order: verb → subject → object
cards.grammarNote:
In a verbal sentence, the most natural order is **Verb – Subject – Object** (VSO):
**أكل الطالب الطعام** (the student ate the food).
Subject-first order (SVO) is also possible but changes emphasis: **الطالب أكل الطعام** = as for the student, he ate the food.

table.title: VSO vs. SVO order in Arabic
table.note: VSO is the default for verbal sentences.

cards.english: In verbal sentence, verb agrees in gender
cards.grammarNote:
When the verb comes before the subject, it agrees in **gender** but stays **singular** even if the subject is plural:
**أكل الطلاب** (the students ate — verb singular because it comes first),
**أكلت الطالبة** (the female student ate — verb feminine).

cloze.prompt: the female student ate (verb-first — feminine verb)

cards.grammarNote:
When the **subject** comes first (as a pronoun), it adds **emphasis or contrast**:
**أنا أعمل هنا** (I — specifically me — work here). Compare: **أعمل هنا** (I work here, neutral).
cards.englishPhrase: I work here (emphasis: me, not someone else).

cards.grammarNote:
**هناك** (hunak, there is/are) begins an existential nominal sentence:
**هناك مطعم قريب** (there is a restaurant nearby), **هناك مطاعم كثيرة** (there are many restaurants).
The noun after **هناك** is always **indefinite**.

produce.task: say: there is a restaurant nearby
produce.answer: هناك مطعم قريب hunak mat'am qarib
produce.gloss: هناك + indefinite مطعم (no ال).

cards.grammarNote:
The past and future tenses do have a 'to be' verb: **كان** (kana = was, m.) / **كانت** (kanat = was, f.):
**كان الطعام لذيذاً** (the food was delicious), **كانت القهوة ساخنة** (the coffee was hot).
The predicate takes accusative (-an) in formal Arabic.

a.gloss: present: the food IS delicious — no verb

b.gloss: past: the food WAS delicious — كان

cards.english: إنّ + noun + pred = emphatic nominal sentence
cards.grammarNote:
**إنّ** (inna) strengthens a nominal sentence — 'indeed / verily':
**إنّ الطعام لذيذ** (the food is indeed delicious).
After **إنّ**, the subject takes the accusative: **إنّ الطعامَ** (note the -a ending on الطعام in formal MSA).

cards.english: هل turns a nominal sentence into a question
cards.grammarNote:
Add **هل** at the start of any sentence (nominal or verbal) to make a yes/no question:
**أنت طالب** (you are a student) → **هل أنت طالب؟** (are you a student?).
No word order change — **هل** just signals the question.

produce.task: turn into a question: الطعام لذيذ
produce.answer: هل الطعام لذيذ؟ hal at-ta'am ladhidh?
produce.gloss: Just add هل to the front — nothing else changes.

cards.english: Question words in nominal vs. verbal sentences
cards.grammarNote:
**Question words** work in both sentence types:
**أين البنك؟** (nominal: where is the bank?), **ماذا تأكل؟** (verbal: what do you eat?), **من هذا الشخص؟** (nominal: who is this person?).

table.title: Question words + sentence type
rows: verbal — what do you eat? (verb present)
verbal — do you work here? (هل + verb)
table.note: أين/من with a noun = nominal; ماذا with a verb = verbal.

cards.grammarNote:
Verbal sentence structure: **verb (agrees in gender) + subject + prepositional phrase**:
**ذهب الطالب إلى المكتبة** (the student went to the library).
Verb agrees with subject in gender: **ذهبت الطالبة** (the female student went).
cards.englishPhrase: The student went to the library.

produce.task: say: the student went to the library
produce.answer: ذهب الطالب إلى المكتبة dhahaba at-talib ila al-maktaba

cards.word: أنا / أنت / هو / هي / نحن / هم
cards.romanized: ana / anta / huwa / hiya / nahnu / hum
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic distinguishes gender in 'you' (2nd person): **أنتَ** (anta, m.) / **أنتِ** (anti, f.).
All other pronouns are shared: **أنا** (I), **هو** (he), **هي** (she), **نحن** (we), **هم** (they m.), **هن** (they f.).
cards.englishPhrase: He works here, she works there.
cards.phrase: هو يعمل هنا، هي تعمل هناك.
cards.phraseRomanized: Huwa ya'mal huna, hiya ta'mal hunak.

cards.grammarNote:
Instead of a separate word for 'my', Arabic attaches a suffix to the noun:
**ـي** (-ī) = my · **ـك** (-ka/-ki) = your · **ـه** (-hu) = his · **ـها** (-ha) = her · **ـنا** (-na) = our.

table.title: Possessive suffixes (on اسم «name»)
table.note: No separate word for 'my' — suffix only.

cards.grammarNote:
**ـي** (-ī) = my, attached directly:
**بيت** (house) → **بيتي** (my house), **مكتب** → **مكتبي** (my office), **اسم** → **اسمي** (my name).
No definite article when a possessive suffix is used.

**ـه** (-hu) = his, attached to the noun:
**اسمه** (his name), **بيته** (his house), **مكتبه** (his office).
Note: after long vowels, the suffix shortens: **في** + **ـه** = **فيه** (in it, m.).

cards.english: Object pronouns: same suffixes on verbs
cards.grammarNote:
The **same suffixes** that mark possession on nouns mark **objects** on verbs:
**يساعدني** (he helps me — suffix **ـني**), **يساعدك** (he helps you — suffix **ـك**), **يساعده** (he helps him — **ـه**).

table.title: Object suffixes on a verb (يساعد = helps)

cards.grammarNote:
Arabic has no verb 'to have'. Instead, use **عند** (at/with) or **لدى** (with/at) + pronoun suffix:
**عندي** ('indi) = I have (lit. 'at me'), **عندك** ('indak) = you have, **عنده** ('indu) = he has.

cards.english: ة → ت when possessive suffix added
cards.grammarNote:
When a possessive suffix is added to a noun ending in **ة**, the **ة** becomes **ت**:
**قهوة** → **قهوتي** (qahwati, my coffee), **طاولة** → **طاولتي** (tawilati, my table), **وجبة** → **وجبتنا** (wajbauna, our meal).

produce.gloss: ة → ت when suffix ي is added.

cards.grammarNote:
**ـنا** (-na) = our: **طاولة** → **طاولتنا** (our table — ة becomes ت before ـنا).
**اسمنا** (ismuna, our name), **بيتنا** (baytuna, our house), **مكتبنا** (maktabuna, our office).

**هذا** (this, m.) · **هذه** (this, f.) — near.
**ذلك** (that, m.) · **تلك** (that, f.) — far.
They agree with the noun's gender: **هذا الكتاب** (this book, m.) · **هذه الطاولة** (this table, f.).

**الذي** (alladhi, who/which, m.) · **التي** (allati, who/which, f.) — used to form relative clauses:
**الطالب الذي يعمل هنا** (the student who works here), **القهوة التي أحب** (the coffee that I like).

Since verb endings show person, **subject pronouns are optional**:
**أعمل** = I work (verb alone is complete), **أنا أعمل** = I (emphatic) work.
Dropping the pronoun is the more neutral, everyday choice.

cards.english: في + suffix = in it / in me
cards.grammarNote:
Prepositions also take the same pronoun suffixes:
**فيه** (in it, m.) · **فيها** (in it, f.) · **فيني** (in me) · **فيك** (in you).
Example: **الشطيرة فيها جبن** (the sandwich has cheese in it).

produce.concept: Preposition + suffix: في + ها = فيها (in it, f.)
produce.task: say: the sandwich has cheese in it (الشطيرة is feminine)
produce.answer: الشطيرة فيها جبن ash-shatira fiha jubn
produce.gloss: فيها = في + ها (feminine 'it').

cards.english: لك (for you m.) / لكِ (for you f.)
cards.grammarNote:
The preposition **لـ** (for/to) + suffix:
**لك** (lak, for you, m.) · **لكِ** (laki, for you, f.) · **له** (lahu, for him) · **لها** (laha, for her).
This mirrors the same distinction in **من فضلك** (to a man) / **من فضلكِ** (to a woman).

cards.english: Arabic has three cases: nominative, accusative, genitive
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic nouns have three grammatical cases indicated by vowel endings:
**رفع** (raf', nominative: subject) = ـُ · **نصب** (nasb, accusative: object/adverb) = ـَ · **جرّ** (jarr, genitive: after preposition/idafa) = ـِ.
In indefinite nouns, these double: tanwin **ـٌ / ـً / ـٍ**.

table.title: Three cases — definite noun
table.note: In everyday speech, final vowels are usually silent.

cards.grammarNote:
The **nominative** (مرفوع) marks the **subject** of a sentence:
**الطالبُ يعملُ** (the student works — الطالب is nominative).
Also the predicate of a nominal sentence: **هو طالبٌ** (he is a student — طالب is nominative predicate).

The **accusative** (منصوب) marks:
1. The **direct object**: **أكلَ الطالبُ الطعامَ** (the student ate the food).
2. **Adverbs** (manner, degree): **جداً** (very), **دائماً** (always), **أيضاً** (also) — all end in tanwin **ـاً**.

table.title: Accusative uses
rows: كان طالباً kana taliban — he was a student
table.note: Indefinite accusative = -an tanwin (ـاً).

cards.english: Genitive (جرّ): after prepositions and in idafa
cards.grammarNote:
The **genitive** (مجرور) marks nouns:
1. **After prepositions**: **في المكتبِ** (in the office), **إلى البيتِ** (to the house).
2. **Second noun in idafa**: **كتابُ الطالبِ** (the student's book — الطالب is genitive).

cloze.prompt: في المكتب — after في the noun takes ___ case

cards.english: Indefinite nouns: tanwin = doubled case vowel
cards.grammarNote:
**Indefinite** nouns add tanwin (doubled case endings):
**ـٌ** (nominative: طالبٌ, 'a student' as subject),
**ـً** (accusative: طالباً, 'a student' as object),
**ـٍ** (genitive: طالبٍ, 'of a student' / after preposition).

table.title: Tanwin — indefinite case endings
table.note: Tanwin is pronounced in formal Arabic, often dropped in speech.

cards.english: Subject vs. object: nominative vs. accusative
cards.grammarNote:
**الطالبُ** (nominative — subject) **يفهمُ** **الطعامَ** (accusative — object).
Note: in **formal/written** Arabic, the case vowels distinguish subject from object. In spoken Arabic, these vowels are usually dropped.

cards.word: من البيتِ / إلى المكتبِ / في الشارعِ
cards.romanized: min al-bayti / ila al-maktabi / fi ash-shari'i
cards.grammarNote:
Every preposition in Arabic takes the **genitive** (مجرور) after it:
**من البيتِ** (from the house), **إلى المكتبِ** (to the office), **في الشارعِ** (in the street), **على الطاولةِ** (on the table).

produce.concept: After any preposition: genitive case (ـِ or tanwin ـٍ)
produce.task: what case does البيت take after من?
produce.gloss: All prepositions (من/إلى/في/على/عن) govern genitive.

cards.grammarNote:
The dual has two forms that show case:
**ـان** (-ān) = nominative (subject): **يدان** (two hands, subject).
**ـين** (-ayn) = accusative/genitive (object/after prep): **لدي يدين** (I have two hands — after لدي).
cards.englishPhrase: I eat two eggs for breakfast.

cards.grammarNote:
The sound masculine plural shows case:
**ـون** (-ūn) = nominative: **المعلمون يعملون** (the teachers work).
**ـين** (-īn) = accusative/genitive: **أرى المعلمين** (I see the teachers).
cards.englishPhrase: The teachers work in the school.

table.title: Sound masc. plural case endings
table.note: ـون drops to ـين when the noun is object or after preposition.

cards.grammarNote:
After **كان** (was), the predicate takes the **accusative** (-an tanwin for indefinite):
**كان طالباً** (he was a student), **كانت المعلمةُ جيدةً** (the teacher was good).
This is one of the key uses of the accusative.

cloze.prompt: he was a student — after كان, predicate takes ___ case

cards.english: Adverbs of manner use accusative tanwin
cards.grammarNote:
Many Arabic adverbs are **frozen accusative** forms (tanwin **ـاً**):
**جداً** (very), **دائماً** (always), **أيضاً** (also), **أبداً** (never).
This is the accusative of specification — the **ـاً** is part of the adverb's fixed form.

produce.task: what ending do جداً / دائماً / أبداً share?
produce.answer: ـاً (-an): accusative tanwin — frozen adverb form
produce.gloss: All end in -an tanwin: jiddan, da'iman, abadan.

cards.english: Case endings: formal/written vs. spoken Arabic
cards.grammarNote:
In **formal/written Arabic** (MSA), case endings are pronounced and written.
In **everyday spoken Arabic**, they are almost always dropped — **الطالب يعمل** (not الطالبُ يعملُ).
The golden rule: learn case endings to read, but don't worry about pronouncing them in conversation.

cards.english: Five negation words — each for a different context
cards.grammarNote:
Arabic uses different negative words depending on **tense and mood**:
**لا** (present/habitual) · **ما** (past, informal) · **لم** + jussive (past) · **لن** + subjunctive (future) · **ليس** (nominal sentences).

table.title: Negation words at a glance
rows: past (formal): لم أذهب (I did not go)
future: لن أذهب (I will not go)
nominal: ليس طبيباً (he is not a doctor)
table.note: Choose based on tense: present/past/future/nominal.

cards.grammarNote:
**لا** (lā) + present-tense verb negates **habitual or present** actions:
**لا أفهم** (I don't understand), **لا يعمل** (he doesn't work), **لا تأكل اللحم** (he/she doesn't eat meat).

**لم** (lam) + **jussive** present negates the **past**:
**لم أذهب** (I did not go), **لم يأكل** (he did not eat), **لم نعمل** (we did not work).
The verb after **لم** is present in form but past in meaning.
cards.englishPhrase: I did not go to the office.

contrast.prompt: لا vs. لم — present or past?

b.gloss: لم + jussive = he did not go (past)

cards.grammarNote:
**لن** (lan) + **subjunctive** present negates the **future**:
**لن أذهب** (I will not go), **لن يعمل** (he will not work), **لن نأكل** (we will not eat).
It is stronger than just 'won't' — carries a firm refusal or certainty.

**ليس** (laysa) negates a **nominal (equational) sentence** — it is a defective verb meaning 'is not':
**هو طبيب** (he is a doctor) → **هو ليس طبيباً** (he is not a doctor).
The predicate after **ليس** takes the **accusative**: **ليس طبيباً** (not *طبيب*).

**ليس** conjugates for gender/number:
**ليس** (m. sg.) · **ليست** (f. sg.) · **لسنا** (we are not) · **ليسوا** (they are not).
**هي ليست طبيبة** (she is not a doctor).

cloze.prompt: she is not — which form of ليس?
cloze.text: هي ___ طالبة (she is not a student)

cards.english: ما + past verb = did not (informal alternative)
cards.grammarNote:
**ما** (mā) + **past tense** verb is an informal/colloquial alternative for past negation:
**ما ذهبتُ** (I didn't go), **ما أكلتُ** (I didn't eat).
In formal MSA, **لم** + jussive is preferred; **ما** + past is common in dialects.

**لا** + **jussive** verb forms a **negative imperative** (don't!):
**لا تذهب!** (don't go!), **لا تأكل!** (don't eat!), **لا تشرب!** (don't drink!).
For a woman: **لا تذهبي** (la tadhhabbi!). For plural: **لا تذهبوا**.

produce.task: say: don't eat! (to a man) and don't drink! (to a man)
produce.answer: لا تأكل! (la ta'kul) / لا تشرب! (la tashrab!)
produce.gloss: لا + jussive (drop the mood vowel from present).

cards.grammarNote:
**أبداً** (abadan) = never/ever, used with a negative verb:
**لا أتأخر أبداً** (I am never late), **لا أشرب الكحول أبداً** (I never drink alcohol).
**أبداً** alone in a response = 'absolutely not / never'.

cards.english: لم vs. لن — past or future?
cards.grammarNote:
**لم** negates the past: **لم أذهب** (I did not go).
**لن** negates the future: **لن أذهب** (I will not go).
Both use the present-tense verb form after them (jussive for **لم**, subjunctive for **لن**).
cards.englishPhrase: I did not eat. I will not eat.

contrast.prompt: لم or لن — past or future?

a.gloss: I did not eat — PAST negation

b.gloss: I will not eat — FUTURE negation

cards.english: لا في + nominal context = no such thing
cards.grammarNote:
**لا** can negate a noun directly in set phrases: **لا مشكلة** (no problem!), **لا شيء** (nothing), **لا شكر على واجب** (don't mention it — lit. 'no thanks for a duty').
These are frozen nominal negations.

table.title: Common لا + noun phrases
table.note: These are fixed expressions; لا negates the noun.

cards.english: Negation review: which word for which tense?
cards.grammarNote:
Quick reference:
**لا** (present/habitual) + indicative verb
**لم** (past formal) + jussive
**لن** (future) + subjunctive
**ليس** (nominal) + predicate in accusative

cards.phrase: لا آكل. لم آكل. لن آكل.

cards.english: She is not a student — which negation?
cards.grammarNote:
For negating a **nominal (equational) sentence**, use **ليس/ليست**:
**هي ليست طالبة** (she is not a student).
Do NOT use **لا** with a noun to negate 'is': **لا** is only for verbs.
